voice.instruct: A friendly software engineer in their thirties walking teammates through a live demo. Clear, warm, neutral international English accent, medium pitch, steady relaxed pace, conversational and confident, never salesy.
voice.reference_text: Let me walk you through how this works. It's simpler than it looks, and I'll show each step as we go.

scenes.say: This is a quick proof of concept. The UI and the BFF live in two separate repositories, and the BFF owns every validation rule. The UI doesn't keep a copy of any of them.

Here's the setup. The shell loads the order form micro frontend. Inside it sits a second micro frontend, the bank form, loaded from its own server. The rules come from the BFF's contracts endpoint, as you can see in the request log.
Error path first. I'll type a five digit account number into the embedded bank form. As soon as I leave the field, the error shows up, because the browser is running the BFF's own rule.

Now the happy path. With a valid ten digit number, the order form submits everything, including the bank details from the embedded form. The BFF checks it again with the same schema, and accepts the order.
Here's the second approach. In server mode, the browser holds no rules at all. When I leave the field, the form asks the BFF's validate endpoint, and shows the very same message.
Valid details pass the same check, and the order goes through.
What if the browser check is skipped entirely? The BFF still rejects the bad data on submit, and points to the exact field.
Last, the BFF team changes the rule from ten digits to twelve, and redeploys only the BFF.
After a reload, the UI enforces the new rule straight away. No micro frontend was rebuilt.
On its own, the bank form uses its own bank form contract from the BFF, separate from the order form's.
So that's the idea. One source of truth in the BFF, a separate contract per micro frontend, and no published package.
